# PNF Is a Whole Conditioning System Built on Five P-Factors, Not Just a Stretching Method

**What it is** — Section 7.2 is Siff's: in 7.5 the book says "the author" gave the 1989 NSCA presentation (Siff, 1989) (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418) and that "An overview of this presentation and workshop acted as the basis for Chapter 7.2 above" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419). He writes that coaches regard PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) as "a special type of sophisticated stretching," but "it is actually an entire system of therapy comprising a broad spectrum of different techniques and procedures," of which stretching is "but one of many aspects" (PDF p. 414 / printed p. 403). History: PNF "was developed by Herman Kabat from 1946-1951" on work by Sherrington, Hellebrand, McGraw and Pavlov (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Definition: "a system for promoting the response of neuromuscular mechanisms by stimulating the proprioceptors"; Knott and Voss say its techniques involve "placing a demand where a response is required," which Siff ties to the SAID principle (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Two types: classical PNF, "the hands-on clinical approach described in the Knott and Voss text," and modified PNF, which "adapts certain PNF techniques and principles for application by hand or apparatus in physical conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). The structure is "five P-factors: Principles, Procedures, Patterns, Positions and Postures, with joint Pivots and Pacing (Timing) as important sub-categories" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Siff lists 23 principles (PDF pp. 416-417 / printed pp. 405-406). Inference: the five groups below are this entry's grouping, not Siff's; the items inside them are his: movement form (spiral and diagonal patterns; motion crossing the sagittal midline; all movement components, flexion-extension, adduction-abduction, internal-external rotation; exercising of related muscle groups (principle 4); multiple joint and muscle action; comfortable full range; appropriate joint positioning); loading (maximal resistance through the range of non-ballistic movement; maximal resistance to promote "overflow (irradiation) of muscle activity from stronger to weaker patterns"; commencement of motion in the strongest range; stronger muscles augmenting the weaker; "Movement free of pain, but not free of effort"); neural (judicious eliciting of reflexes; sensory cues; visuo-motor and audio-motor coordination; agonists and antagonists; static and dynamic conditions; repeated contractions for motor learning); progression (primitive to complex; each phase laying foundations for the next; all activities integrated and goal directed); and adjuncts (cold, electrostimulation, massage, vibration, stroking). Positions and postures hold some joints stable so "All action can then take place around specific joints as pivots"; pacing ("normal timing") is "the timing of the phases of a movement or series of movements which occur naturally in an uninjured, healthy person" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image). Quotes from PDF pp. 414-418 are from the text layer.

**Why it works** — Siff's rationale is that "all physical conditioning depends primarily on neuromuscular processes involving sensitive receptors (proprioceptors) in the muscles, tendons and joints," so "Appropriate recruitment of the various stretch reflexes of the body ... forms a vital part of PNF conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Muscle contraction "is really the end-product of the interaction of various voluntary and reflex neuromotor processes," and bodybuilding-style training "over-emphasizes the role of muscle contraction" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). He names the reflexes used: the phasic and tonic components of the myotatic stretch reflex (short and long duration stretching loads give different responses), the Golgi tendon reflex to "reduce the tension in a muscle and promote local relaxation," and reciprocal inhibition, which "can produce a significantly stronger contraction of the agonists" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Maximal contraction through the range ensures "summation," the adding of motor-unit twitches by more units or a higher firing rate (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404).

**When to apply** — Use the 23 principles as a checklist when designing or reviewing supplementary exercises: Siff says "employment of any of the above principles in training implies conscious or unconscious reliance on aspects of the PNF system" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). His own scope claim: PNF can improve "all the S-factors of fitness ... except cardiovascular endurance and psychological fitness" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405; see [[framework--s-factors-pyramidal-fitness-model]]). Positions as pivots matter in ordinary lifts: a dumbbell curl "with the elbow dug firmly into the side" produces "activation patterns and results which are distinctly different" from one with elbow and shoulder free, and the unrestrained curl adds cheating, trapezius involvement and "downward traction ... at the shoulder joint" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). The 7.4 opening makes a related point about the same lift: "'bicep curls' do not involve the brachial biceps only, but also the brachialis and brachialis to differing degrees, depending on hand position and speed of movement" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416, checked against the page image; the doubled "brachialis" is printed so). The 7.4.1 summary lists elbow flexion as "Brachialis, brachioradialis (particularly if the movement is rapid). Also biceps (if forearm is supinated) and pronator teres (if forearm is pronated)" (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418, checked against the page image). Inference: the second "brachialis" in the 7.4 sentence is probably meant to be brachioradialis, which the 7.4.1 list names. Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the PNF principles fit best in that small assistance share and in Athletic Medicine handoffs, where multi-joint diagonal patterns can replace single-joint machine work.

**When NOT to apply** — Siff's case that PNF is a complete athletic conditioning system is argued, not tested: he gives no training study, and "No training method could be required to offer much more than this repertoire to qualify as an all-round conditioning system" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405) is a judgment. The patterns "were devised for rehabilitation, not elite sporting training" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410), so strict PNF is not the goal for athletes (see [[principle--train-for-a-safety-factor-above-competition-forces]]). Two source oddities: the principles say "Use of distal to proximal sequences in neuromuscularly mature subjects" (principle 18) while the developmental list gives "proximal to distal, distal to proximal" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405); and procedure 4 attributes the stretch reflex in the lengthened range to "Starling's Law" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). Inference: Starling's law is usually stated for cardiac muscle; the book gives no explanation of the link. Classical PNF is hands-on clinical work; Siff points coaches to the NSCA videotapes (Siff, 1989) rather than describing every technique (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).

**Example** — From 7.5: a coach applying the 7.2 list to a baseball pitcher or javelin thrower, instead of the pec-deck, "would recommend the use of a pulley machine in a specific spiral-diagonal pattern (see 7.2.3.1) of cable-crossovers that cross the sagittal midline of the body," performed "over a comfortable full range," involving "multiple joints besides just the shoulder" with joints positioned "to optimise strengthening" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Figs 7.3-7.8 (PDF pp. 419-420 / printed pp. 408-409, checked against the page images) draw the upper-extremity, lower-extremity and trunk patterns, each labelled with its three component motions (for example "Flexion to Extension, Abduction to Adduction, Ext to Int Rotation").

**Related** — [[framework--pnf-activation-and-relaxation-techniques]], [[claim--novices-progress-from-mobility-to-stability-pnf-sequence]], [[heuristic--use-pulleys-and-dumbbells-for-spiral-diagonal-pnf-patterns]], [[claim--functional-training-means-sport-specific-and-no-exercise-is-non-functional]], [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]] (the reflexes PNF uses, Fig 3.33), [[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (the overflow principle), [[framework--stretching-techniques-taxonomy-static-vs-dynamic]] (PNF as a stretching category, 3.5.8), [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]] (PNF use of the positive supportive reaction)

## Verdict

**GO AFTER FIXES**

The source reading is strong. Checked against the images:
- All 24 bullets of the 8.10 machine list (12 on PDF 481, 9 on PDF 482, 3 on PDF 483), and the grouping keeps every item.
- The 90% Chaffin & Andersson figure and its seated-versus-standing framing (PDF 481).

The caption-versus-figure mismatch ("very short" is not a set label) is real.
- Farfel et al (1975) quoted word for word, including "(Sokolov, 1982)", "Masters of Sport Class" and "errors of as much as 100% were common".

The fixes are:
- five missing cross-links to existing entries that already carry the same idea (one of them is a Basmajian point the entry should reconcile);
- one unflagged misprint ("see 1.14" for the energy systems, which are 1.15);
- one wrong justification for the single `supported` rating (the rating itself stands);

|---|---|---|
| PDF 489 cites the shoe and belt material as "(8.8)" and "(Ch 8.8)" | Confirmed: "As discussed earlier (8.8), shoes can alter the proprioceptive sensitivity of the foot..." and "The correct use of the weightlifting belt ... was also discussed earlier (Ch 8.8)." Both are in 8.9 (8.9.2 and 8.9.1, PDF 478-480) | `heuristic--use-touch...`: correct ("both are in 8.9 in this edition"). `_book.md` 8.12 row: correct. `claim--lifting-belt-cues...` quotes the PDF 489 sentence without the "(Ch 8.8)" tag and says only "Later in the chapter the book points back to", which is accurate |

| Not reported, handled: "helps keeps the flat" (PDF 478), "detect in the soft tissues of athletes that may be" (PDF 488), "and not the wave-like transitions" (PDF 486) | Confirmed | Each is noted correctly in its entry (`claim--lifting-belt-cues...`, `heuristic--keep-all-staff...`, `framework--four-types-of-stability...`, the last with "Inference:") |

## Farfel et al (1975): is `supported` justified?

**Yes, at the lower bound, for the observation only.** The book's own paragraph (PDF 490 / p.479) describes the study rather than merely citing it. It gives:
- the aim (to find what information force control is based on);
- the population class (elite Russian weightlifters, Masters of Sport Class);
- the instrument (special pulling dynamometers);
- the conditions (static and explosive; different lifts and stages; estimates relative to the felt 1RM);
- the result (errors "of as much as 100% were common");
- the conclusion.

No other cited study in 8d gets that much. Kovalik, Robbins et al, Basmajian and Vorobyev's 40% are all one-line citations and are rightly `untested`.

Against it:
- There is no n, no error distribution and no protocol detail.
- The single figure is a ceiling called "common".
- The report is second-hand through Sokolov (1982).
- The book calls Masters of Sport "even world class", which overstates the group.

So the rating holds only for "elite lifters' estimates of exerted force were often badly wrong". It does not hold for the causal conclusion (that "inappropriate training methods" caused it) or for the biofeedback remedy, which the entry already marks as untested.

The justification sentence is wrong, though. The entry says the rating follows "the standard the 8c review applied to partly described Vorobyev data". That standard was printed tabular data with stated conditions, and Farfel has no printed data. See fix 9.

=== claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max
# The Authors Locate Endurance in the Muscles' Oxidative and Strength Qualities Rather Than in VO2 Max, but Give Conflicting Advice on Glycolytic Work

**What it is** — Under "Oxidative Capacity and Muscular Endurance" (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249, verified against the page image), the authors cite research that endurance gains are "associated more with enhancing the ability of the muscles to utilise a higher percentage of the oxygen already in the blood than with increasing the amount of oxygen in the bloodstream" (Ekblom 1969; Rowell 1971; Saltin 1974). "A rise in intramuscular energy potential, the power of the oxidative processes and the contractile (strength) qualities of the muscles decrease the rate of glycolysis" (four citations), and lactate falls "in the skeletal muscles and not in the liver and myocardium, as has always been believed" (Jorfeldt 1970; Knutten 1971; Gollnick & Hermansen 1973). Their italicised conclusion: "the development of endurance is associated with functional specialisation of the skeletal muscles, particu

**Why it works** — The mechanism the authors give: stronger, more oxidative muscle relies less on glycolysis, makes less lactate and oxidises more of it in the muscle itself. They support it with citations, not with data shown in the text.

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism in this passage. Inference: it follows from their preceding argument that endurance depends on the muscles' strength and oxidative qualities (see Related), but they do not state that link here.

hypertrophy: an increase in the size and number of sarcomeres within myofibrils; when

=== heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed
# Time Restoration to When Work Capacity Is Next Needed: Immediately for the Same Day, 6-9 Hours Later for Tomorrow; Whole-Body After General Work, Local After Local

**What it is** — Talyshev's (1977) conclusion from his timing study: "work capacity and its magnitude depend strongly on the time at which the restorative methods are applied. When an immediate effect is necessary, namely when the greatest work capacity recovery after a short span of time is needed (e.g. between morning and afternoon workouts), it is advisable to employ restorative methods immediately after workouts or morning starts. If, however, a high work capacity is required on the following day, then it is better to employ recovery methods 6-9 hours after the workout or competition. If the workout or competition ends late in the evening, it is preferable to start recovery procedures in the morning, shortly after awakening" (PDF 462 / p.451, checked against the page image). A second rule from "Related work": "it is best to employ full-body recovery methods (e.g. sauna, hydrotherapy,

**Why it works** — The basis is the study (see [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]]): immediate therapy raised work capacity for a few hours but left it below baseline the next day, while therapy at 6-9 hours produced next-day supercompensation (PDF 462). The authors' framing: recovery is fastest straight after exercise, so it is "more advisable to accelerate recovery processes when their natural rate is slowing down" (PDF 462).

=== claim--strength-endurance-hypertrophy-and-cyclic-endurance
# Strength-Endurance Helps Cyclic Endurance, but Some Popular Strength Exercises and Excess Hypertrophy Hinder It; Never Let Relative Strength Fall

**What it is** — From 5.2.5 (PDF pp. 297-298 / printed pp. 286-287, verified against the page images):
- "an increase in strength-endurance contributes to improving endurance in distance runners, skiers and skaters (Popov, 1968; Nabatnikova, 1972; Mikhailov & Panov, 1975). However ... the magnitude of the strength load used is different if, on the one hand, the key quality required is general endurance and, on the other hand, it is strength-endurance."
- "certain popular strength exercises such as running with a sack of sand weighing 25% of the subject's bodyweight, barbell pressing, squats, 'good mornings', and twisting with a barbell not only do not enhance, but to a certain degree, will even hinder the development of endurance in cyclic type exercises (Maisuradze, 1960)." In some instances "the increase in strength is associated with excessive muscle hypertrophy". "Endurance and hypertrophy do not increase simultaneously and there is no correlation between them (Maison & Broeker, 1941; McMorris & Elkins, 1954)."
- No definite correlation between special strength and muscle mass in cyclic endurance sports (middle distance running, skating, skiing: Chistyakov, 1965; Chernyaev, 1965; Nabatnikova, 1972). But in gymnasts "a positive linear correlation (R = 0.77) is noticed between strength-endurance and relative strength (Zhalei, 1964). Therefore, in those cases where endurance is associated with the display of significant strength, some muscular hypertrophy does not negatively influence training results."
- Closing rules: "Strength training should not result in increased muscle mass in those types of sport where the key quality is endurance of moderate work output. If strength-endurance is required, especially in those cases where it is necessary to overcome a large resistance, a small increase in muscle mass is permissible. In no cases, should the training ever produce a decrease in relative strength of any muscle groups in the body" (PDF p. 298 / printed p. 287).

**Tension with Chapter 4, recorded:** section 4.4 cites research that strength training "contributes more to the largest improvements in distance sports than aerobic training" (PDF pp. 261-262 / printed pp. 250-251; see [[claim--strength-training-raises-haemoglobin-myoglobin-and-aids-distance-sport]]), while 5.2.5 says squats, presses and good mornings "will even hinder the development of endurance in cyclic type exercises" (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286). Inference: the two may differ in which strength exercises and loads are meant, but the book does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation is the hypertrophy by-product and the lack of correlation between endurance and hypertrophy; they give no physiology beyond that.

**What it is** — The authors give the durations "vital for maximal enhancement of the body's CAR" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349, checked against the page image):
1. "the appropriate duration of continuous training is 5-6 weeks, and with concentrated loading, the duration is 3-4 weeks, after which a recuperation period is necessary for activating the compensatory processes."
2. "the trained athlete is able to tolerate three such sequential blocks of loading, separated by short recuperation pauses (7-10 days). After this, a longer recuperation period is necessary to facilitate stabilisation at the new level of adaptation."
3. "Thus, the time interval necessary for exhausting the body's CAR is between 18-22 weeks (see Fig 6.23). This period coincides with observations of highly qualified athletes training in different sports, including cyclic types (Zhikharevich, 1976; Sirenko, 1980)."
4. "the body cannot indefinitely continue to adapt successively to training loads," and "it is inappropriate to subject the body to extreme exhaustion of its energy reserves. This requires a longer recuperation period and has a negative effect on the subsequent stages of adaptation."

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the CAR model: each block draws on a limited reserve, the recuperation pause lets the compensatory reaction occur, and after about three blocks the reserve is spent (see [[principle--load-must-sit-within-the-current-adaptation-reserve-window]]). No data for the durations are shown beyond the two citations for the 18-22 week period.

# Long-Term Adaptation Runs on Two Linked Functions: Energy Provision for External Work and Plastic Provision for Repair (Fig 1)

**What it is** — The Addendum (9.1) is Yuri Verkhoshansky's own paper, translated by Michael Yessis (byline, PDF 515 / p.504). In the introduction (9.1 Introduction, PDF 517 / p.506, checked against the page image) he writes: "The 'long term' adaptation mechanism is comprised of the energy and plastic providing functions of the body together with their mutual conditioning effect." The energy function is the "joining of the metabolic processes" that releases enough energy for the needed level of activity. "The plastic provision is a process of repair of the functional, energy forming, transport and support structures of the cells. It is realized through protein biosynthesis." He then takes a systems view from Bauer and Kasnacheev: "the state of the biological system is determined by interaction between two main energy flows: the first is used to attain the maximal effect of 'external work' (energy ensuring function), and the second flow is used to attain restitution of the energy ensuring macro- and micro structures (plastic provision function)" (PDF 517 / p.506). Figure 1 (V.P. Kasnacheev, 1980; PDF 517, read from the image) plots the relative energy share to external work (axis I) against the share to restitution (axis II). A shaded band labelled "Normal ratio" sits between two lines labelled "Limit of compensation." Curve a oscillates inside the band ("the normal correlation"); curves b and c leave it, b running out along the restitution side and c shooting up the external-work side ("the compensational limits").

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's account: at rest, with no "adaptogenic factor," the two processes fluctuate "within normal limits of physiological fluctuations (see Figure 1 graph a)." When the factor is present, "the amplitude of oscillation in the alternation of the energetic and plastic providing functions increases. However, it is only up to a certain physiological limit after which there inevitably is a disturbance in the adaptational mechanism" (PDF 517-518 / p.506-507). He adds that "in separate stages one or another process can dominate, and even in micro intervals of time, a balance between them is maintained" (PDF 518 / p.507). Footnote 2 (PDF 517, unsigned glossary note) gives Bauer's "principle of the permanent non-equilibrium of living matter" and his two "general biological lows" (printed so; the sense is laws): systems develop by increasing their external working effect, and because they are "constantly working and destructing," they must restore themselves from the environment.

**When to apply** — As a frame for reading any session: part of the response spends energy on the work, part rebuilds the structures used. Inference: this is the frame Verkhoshansky uses later in 9.1 to argue that the rest interval belongs to plastic provision (see [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]) and to draw the energetic and plastic phases of his three adaptation strategies (see [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Figure 1 is a schematic with no units, no data and no stated sample; it comes from Kasnacheev's general biology, not from sport studies. The text does not say how far a training load can push the oscillation before the "disturbance" begins, so the model cannot set a dose. The Bauer footnote is a glossary note, not Verkhoshansky's argument, and Bauer's "non-equilibrium" biology (1935) is cited as theory. Treat the frame as a way of thinking, not a measured result.

**Example** — Fig 1 itself (PDF 517 / p.506): curve a stays inside the "Normal ratio" band, while b and c cross the "Limit of compensation" lines, the two ways the balance can fail.

**Related** — [[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]], [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--compensatory-adaptation-is-temporary-and-precedes-stable-adaptation]] (6.8.1)

# Small, Familiar Loads Stay Within Specific Homeostatic Reactions; Larger or Longer Loads Switch On the General (Stress) Adaptation Mechanism (Viru, Fig 2)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, using Viru's scheme (9.1 Introduction, PDF 518-519 / p.507-508, checked against the page images): "Management of the adaptation process is done by the CNS (Figure 2)." Its first result is "the activation of specific homeostatic reactions." "When the strength (level) of the irritants is not high and the changes in the external and internal environment is not great, and in the presence of the previously worked out adaptation to a given action, the adaptational effect is limited to the specifics of the homeostatic reactions." As the strength and duration of the influence rise, the cells' own energy and plastic capabilities "require support from the side of general mobilization of the energy and plastic reserves of the body. This means mobilization of the non-specific component of adaptation or (according to Viru) inclusion of the general adaptation mechanism." That activation "appears as the basic sign of the stress state." Figure 2 ("The scheme of the mechanism of general adaptation (Viru, 1981)", PDF 518, read from the image) runs Stressor, then CNS, then two branches: "Specific homeostatic" and "General Adaptation." General adaptation splits into "Mobilization of energy reserve and energy provisioning functions," "Mobilisation of plastic resources and adaptive synthesis of enzymatic and structural proteins" and "Activation of defenses faculties (immunoactivities, etc..)," with "Ensuring the work of ionic pumps" feeding back to the specific reactions and "Ensuring the transition to the long term adaptation" linked back by a dashed line.

**Why it works** — The hormonal division of labour he gives, citing Viru (32, 289) and Yakovlev (144): "In mobilization of the energy resources of the body and in the energy provision function, predominant importance is given to the sympatho-adrenal system," acting through "hormonal (adrenaline) and mediatory (noradrenaline) links." "Mobilization of the plastic reserve of the body under stress is a function of the hypophyseal-adrenocortical system," tied to "the creation of a free amino acid reserve" for adaptive protein synthesis (PDF 519 / p.508). In the adapted body "there is increased power of the mechanism of the hormonal - humoral regulation," which "increases the maximum reaction of the body to limit loads, that ensures maximum mobilization of its functional capabilities" (PDF 519 / p.508).

**When to apply** — Inference: use the two branches to judge what a session asks for. A familiar, moderate session in a trained athlete stays in the specific branch and mostly maintains; a new, heavier or longer load recruits the general stress response, which is what funds new structure. This frames why Verkhoshansky ties progressive adaptation to loads that "bring about systematic disturbance of body homeostasis" (PDF 521 / p.510; see [[claim--compensatory-adaptation-is-temporary-and-precedes-stable-adaptation]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The page gives no thresholds: "not high" and "not great" are not quantified, so the scheme cannot tell a coach where one branch ends. It is a cited model (Viru 1981), shown without data. The stress-state framing follows Selye (cited on PDF 516), so the same caution applies as in the 8.5 overtraining entry: "stress" here is a whole-body hormonal state, not only fatigue. Inference: modern work adds local signalling (mechanical tension, for example) that this hormone-centred scheme does not show.

**Example** — Fig 2 (PDF 518 / p.507): the stressor reaches the CNS, which can answer through the specific homeostatic box alone or also through the three general-adaptation boxes, one of which leads on to "Ensuring the transition to the long term adaptation."

**Related** — [[framework--bauer-kasnacheev-energy-and-plastic-flows-fig-1]], [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--car-volume-is-capped-and-shrinks-as-mastery-nears-the-genetic-limit]] (the same two hormonal systems cap the reserve), [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]] (8.5, Selye's stress)

# Acute Adaptation Works at the Body's Limits; Only Repeated Bouts That Switch On Protein Synthesis Build Long-Term Adaptation

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, citing Kusnetzov, Meerson, Haydarliu and Viru (9.1 Introduction, PDF 516 / p.505, checked against the page image): "there are two stages in development of the adaptational process: the beginning stage - 'acute' (short term), incomplete adaptation, and the following stage - 'long term', completed adaptation." The acute stage starts at once and so "could be realized only on the basis of the earlier formed physiological mechanisms." "The most important trait of this stage of adaptation is that the activity of the body takes place on the limits of its physiological abilities, during almost full mobilization of the functional reserves, which are still far from the full measure needed to ensure the necessary adaptational effect." The long-term stage "appears gradually as a result of long or multiple repetitions" and "is developed on the basis of multiple realizations of 'acute' adaptation," until the body "acquires a new quality - a level of functional abilities that is greater than earlier." He calls the transition "the main moment in the adaptational process" (PDF 516 / p.505). Section 1.1 restates it for sport: "Short term adaptation transitions gradually into long term on the basis of multiple short term and systematic training effects on the body (training days, training sessions)" (9.1 §1.1, PDF 521 / p.510).

**Why it works** — The bridge is protein synthesis: "an increase in the function of organs and systems naturally entail the activation of the synthesis of nucleic acid and cell proteins that form these organs and systems," producing structural changes that "appear as a quality material base on which the formation and transition from 'short' to 'long term' adaptation is realized" (PDF 516 / p.505). In 1.2 he ties this to the reserve: "The realization of CAR to the limits that it can be withstood, activates the genetic apparatus of inner cellular regulation," leading to structural changes "ensuring the transition from short term adaptation to long term (Meerson, 76-77, Viru, 32,33)" (9.1 §1.2, PDF 522 / p.511). He lists the transfer "through activation of the genetic apparatus of the cells and the induction of adaptive protein synthesis" among the findings of the adaptation literature (PDF 516 / p.505).

**When to apply** — When explaining why one hard session changes little and a block changes a lot: a single bout spends reserves, and the structure is built only by repeated bouts. Inference: a coach judging a block by the first week's response is reading the acute stage, which by this account is still "far from the full measure."

**When NOT to apply** — The section is a literature summary with citations and no data shown. **Example** — Verkhoshansky's own wording of the sport case: "training days, training sessions" are the "multiple short term and systematic training effects" through which short-term adaptation "transitions gradually into long term" (PDF 521 / p.510).

# Training Theory as a Hierarchy: Laws of Adaptation, Then Laws of Sports Mastery, Then Principles, Then the Time Forms of Training (Fig 3)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky opens 9.1 with the "multi year Process of Achieving Sports Mastery (PASM)," which "was developed on a base of definite laws. Athletes can achieve the heights of sports mastery by different pathways and expend different amounts of time doing this. However, the path taken by each athlete will have general traits, inherent to all athletes," set by "genetically imposed abilities of the body to accommodate" (9.1 Introduction, PDF 515 / p.504, checked against the page image). "The general laws of PASM are first of all determined by the laws of development of the adaptational process related to sports activity (Figure 3)" (PDF 519 / p.508). Figure 3 ("The principal structure of the fundamentals of the Theory and Methodology of Sport Training," PDF 520 / p.509, read from the image; no source is given) stacks: "The laws of adaptation"; "General laws of PASM"; two branches, "The laws of the morphological-functional specialization" and "The laws of the technical and tactical mastery perfectioning"; between them "Principles to develop the training process"; then "The forms of the temporal organization of training," which divide into "Yearly cycle," "Large training cycle," "Micro-cycle," "Training day" and "Training seance" (printed so).

**Why it works** — His argument: "The general laws of the PASM reflect the necessary structure of multiyear training in an objective manner, including the order of development of all of its components and the principles of their interactions." The principles are "joined with the objective display of the practical realization of the laws of adaptation of the body to loaded muscular activity, to determine the organizational-temporal form of constructing sports training" (PDF 520 / p.509). Other drivers of mastery, "socio-economic conditions, effectiveness of the theoretical concept of training, professional mastery of the coach, the individual psycho-physiological personality traits of the athlete and so on," are, "even with the indubitable significance of these factors, ... secondary. They can be looked at (and realized) under the process of PASM, but do not determine the principle mechanisms of its development" (PDF 519-520 / p.508-509).

**When to apply** — As an order of questions when building or auditing a plan: what adaptation is wanted, what the sport's specialisation and technical demands require, which principles follow, and only then how to lay out years, blocks, weeks, days and sessions. Inference: the figure puts the calendar last, which is the reverse of building a plan by filling a template of weeks.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states that "It has been proven that the unique correct path to the formulation of effective practical principles of sports training is through the clarification of the laws of human body adaptation" (PDF 519 / p.508), but the page cites his own and colleagues' work, not a test of that claim; it is his position, rated `untested` here. The figure has no source line and no data. Inference: for a team-sport staff, the factors he calls "secondary" (coach skill, the athlete's personality, budgets and schedules) often set the real limits, so the hierarchy describes the logic of a plan, not what most constrains it.

**Example** — Fig 3 (PDF 520 / p.509): the five time forms at the bottom, from "Yearly cycle" down to the single "Training seance," all hang from "The forms of the temporal organization of training," which hangs from the principles and, above them, the laws of adaptation.

# Matveev's Phases of Sports Form Came From Prokop's Adaptation-Energy Phases, Without the Physiology

**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.2, Verkhoshansky notes that "even at the end of the 1950's, the concept of adaptation energy (adaptation ability) disbursement during stress, together with its possible restoration, was used to explain the dynamics of sports achievements during training. Three phases were determined: 1. Phase of adaptation (increase in the athlete's abilities); 2. Phase of the highest sports workability; 3. Phase of readaptation (Prokop, 258)" (9.1 §1.2, PDF 522 / p.511, checked against the page image). Footnote 3 on the same page (unsigned) adds: "This idea was subsequently adopted by L.Matveev, who interpreted these phases as the phases of formation, stabilization and loss of sports form without any kind physiological explanation (Matveev L.P. 'The problem of periodization of sports training'. Moscow, 'Physical Culture and Sport', 1965)."

**Why it works** — The point of the footnote: the three-phase shape of classical periodisation (build form, hold it, lose it) began as a description of spending and restoring a limited adaptation energy under stress. Inference: by this account the phases were the visible trace of a reserve being used up and rebuilt, and Matveev kept the trace while dropping the reserve, which is the cause Verkhoshansky builds his own CAR model on (see [[claim--car-volume-is-capped-and-shrinks-as-mastery-nears-the-genetic-limit]]).

**When to apply** — When reading or teaching the history of periodisation, and when a "loss of sports form" phase is treated as a fixed calendar step rather than as the result of a spent reserve. Inference: the footnote gives a reason to plan the "readaptation" phase by the state of the athlete, not by date.

**When NOT to apply** — The footnote is a one-line attribution with no evidence and no page reference into Matveev's book, and it is not signed; it reads as Verkhoshansky's side in a long dispute with Matveev (see [[claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov]]). Matveev's own account of where the phases came from is not given. Rated `untested`. Inference: whether Matveev offered "any kind" of physiological explanation would need his 1965 book, which is not in this library.

**Example** — The three Prokop phases on PDF 522 / p.511 set against Matveev's "formation, stabilization and loss of sports form" in footnote 3 on the same page.

# Three Adaptation Strategies: Moderate Loads, High Loads Spread Evenly, High Loads Concentrated (Fig 4)

**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.3, "The adaptation strategy," Verkhoshansky defines strategy as "a form and means of realizing the laws of adaptation in practical sports conditions" and gives "three variants of adaptational strategy that have been studied and written up (figure 4)" (Verkhoshansky, 24; Verkhoshansky & Viru, 28, 286) (9.1 §1.3, PDF 522-524 / p.511-513, checked against the page images):
- **A, low-middle loads.** "If moderate volume and intensity training loads are used (in relation to the current state of the athlete) then for specialized workability (W) it is characteristic to have moderate and relatively balanced development." "Full exhaustion of CAR does not take place and the adaptational process is extended over time. This type of strategy is for beginning and mid level athletes." Afterwards W can go three ways: "a decrease (if there is a decrease in the strength of the training influences), stabilization (if so called maintenance loads are used) or further increases (if the strength of the training influences are increased)" (PDF 523 / p.512).
- **B, high loads distributed evenly**, "the traditional variant of organization of high level athlete training." It "ensures periodic short term disturbance of the constant internal body environment"; the process is "on a more intense level and its duration has a definite limit." Afterwards only two ways: "a decrease (even if the volume and intensity of the loads increases)" or "stabilization (if maintenance loads are used)" (PDF 523-524 / p.512-513).
- **C, high loads concentrated in a short period.** "The beginning stage of training is distinguished by systematic long term and deep disturbance of body homeostasis due mainly to the mobilization of the energy resources," seen as a "steady decrease in specialized workability (W)." Then, "as a result of mainly mobilization of the plastic resources," comes "a sharply expressed increase," to "a significant increase above the initial level and even the level achieved in the first two variants." Afterwards: "a decrease (if once again concentrated load volumes are used)" or "continued stabilization (if maintenance loads are used)" (PDF 524 / p.513).

Figure 4 (PDF 523 / p.512, values read from the image): panel A has no numeric scale. In B, W% rises from 100 to about 140 by week 10 and levels near 150 by week 20. In C, W% falls to about 80 near week 5, crosses 100 near week 9, and levels near 155 by about weeks 17-20. Each panel ends in tails a and b (A also c) after week 20. Hatched down-arrows mark the loading and open up-arrows the rebound.

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's mechanism is the energy-plastic alternation (see [[framework--bauer-kasnacheev-energy-and-plastic-flows-fig-1]]): in A "consecutive alternation of moderate activation of the energetic (solid line) and plastic (dotted line) reserves"; in B "the expenditure of the energetic resources (solid lines) is compensated for by the mobilization of the plastic resources (dash lines)"; in C a long energy-dominated phase is followed by a plastic-dominated phase (PDF 523-524). Figure note: the text refers to solid, dotted and dash lines, but the printed Fig 4 shows one curve per panel with hatched and open arrows and no line legend. Inference: the down-arrows stand for energetic mobilisation and the up-arrows for plastic mobilisation.

**When to apply** — Use A for beginners and mid-level athletes, where CAR need not be exhausted. Use C only where the athlete is highly qualified, the block can be protected from competition, and a planned dip in W is acceptable. In every variant, plan what follows the block: maintenance loads hold the level, and in B even more load does not raise it.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested` because the C-over-B claim is the same claim the existing 6.8.1 entry carries, which Issurin (2016) contests for team, combat and swimming sports (see [[framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation]]). Fig 4 is a schematic: there is no sample, sport or test named for W, and A has no scale. Inference: the planned dip of about 20% in C would collide with a competition schedule in a field sport. Eric's review: Eric's stated preference differs from both B and C: "waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: that is a difference in approach to record, not a conflict over the same claim.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own contrast in Fig 4 (PDF 523 / p.512): over the same 20 weeks, B rises steadily to about 150%, while C first drops to about 80% and then finishes near 155%.

**Related** — [[framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation]] (6.8.1, Fig 6.23, the two-form version with data), [[principle--mesocycle-not-microcycle-as-the-unit-and-planned-dips-are-not-errors]], [[claim--car-volume-is-capped-and-shrinks-as-mastery-nears-the-genetic-limit]], [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]]

# What Breaks Down During Work Decides What Is Built After It: Metabolites Induce Adaptive Protein Synthesis, Hormones Amplify It

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, citing Yakovlev and Viru throughout (9.1 §1.4, PDF 524 / p.513, checked against the page image): "Synthesis of proteins is provided for by the genetic program coordinated in the nucleus of the cell. Its realization activates the action of the inductors." "The basic inductors appear to be the cell metabolites (products of substance exchange in the cells) and hormones, reaching the cells via the blood." "Metabolites determine the specific character of the protein synthesis; synthesized are those proteins which are primarily destroyed, and likewise enzymes catalyzing biochemical reactions, lying in the base of the corresponding functions." "Hormones as a rule strengthen adaptive protein synthesis, inducted by metabolites." His summary: "the catabolic processes that take place in the muscles during the time of work determine the specific character of the following biosynthesis of the substances destroyed during muscular activity, that is, the specificity of the anabolic processes that take place in the post work period" (PDF 524 / p.513). He repeats it in 1.5: "Metabolites accumulated at the time of work, acts as inductors of adaptive protein synthesis. Hormones actively secreted in these conditions strengthen protein synthesis, specifically directed by metabolites, and assures the supplying of this process by 'constructive materials'" (PDF 528 / p.517).

**Why it works** — Two supporting pieces on PDF 527 / p.516. Gene repression: the muscle fibre carries the genes for all its proteins, but "part of the genetics can be 'repressed'"; under "trophic influence of the nervous system or some kind of change in the conditions, the existing suppression can be lifted and then the muscle can synthesize the proteins, which before this, were not capable of being synthesized" (Yakovlev, 144). Glucocorticoids: they mobilise protein, create "a reserve of free amino acids for ensuring the plastic functions," and move amino acids from one tissue to another, so "the plastic reserves of the cells can be exhausted in some tissues because of the stronger slow of plastic materials" (printed so; Inference: probably "outflow") "and in others as a consequence of more intense use of free resources in the anabolic processes" (Viru). Footnote 9 (PDF 528, quoting Viru 1995, ch. 8) gives the proposed signal: "low molecular weight products of protein degradation" acting on transcription, with specific activation if they "are protein specific fragments."

**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky draws the programming rule from it (PDF 532 / p.521): "Training can be considered effective when the loads bring about induction of adaptive protein synthesis in the desired direction. The criteria for such loads should (or can) be the accumulation of metabolites or the changes in the hormonal ensemble, necessary for specific induction of the adaptive synthesis of protein and for its strengthening (Viru, 289)." Inference: pick the session's means so the breakdown it causes is the breakdown of the structures you want rebuilt.

**When NOT to apply** — The section is a review of cited work (Viru, Yakovlev, Booth, Poortemans and others) with no data on the page. Inference: modern muscle biology also gives a large role to mechanical signalling, which this metabolite-and-hormone account does not mention, so treat it as one part of the mechanism. The page names no practical measure of "the accumulation of metabolites" or "the hormonal ensemble," so the effective-load criterion cannot be applied directly in a weight room.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own strength case (PDF 528 / p.517): hypertrophy from strength training "is based on the strengthened protein synthesis ... and is combined with an increase in the protein content, in mainly the myofibrils," and "the anabolic acting androgenic hormones strengthen this aggregate change (Viru, 33)."

**Related** — [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]], [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]], [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]]

# Each Training Direction Builds Its Own Proteins: Speed the Sarcoplasmic Reticulum, Strength the Contractile Proteins, Endurance the Mitochondria (Table 1)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.4, PDF 525 / p.514, checked against the page image): "The specific character of the biochemical adaptation in the process of training depends to a significant degree, on the essentials of the training loads used (Yakovlev, 140)." Table 1, "Specific influence of different regimes of muscle work on the adaptive synthesis of proteins (According to A. Viru, 1995)," read from the image:

| Primary direction of the training influence | The specific character of the adaptational protein synthesis |
|---|---|
| Development of speed | Synthesis of proteins in the sarcoplasmatic reticulum |
| Development of strength | Synthesis of contractile proteins |
| Development of endurance | Synthesis of mitochondrial proteins |
| Development of speed endurance | Synthesis of proteins with buffering properties, synthesis of isoenzymes resistant to lower pH |

The text below the table restates it by exercise type: "In strength exercises, the myofibril protein synthesis appears to be foremost. In short term exercises of maximum effort there is synthesis of sarcoplasmatic reticulum; in submaximal exercises tied in with insufficient satisfaction of the needed oxygen, accumulation of non-oxidized metabolites, and a change in pH to the acid side, there is synthesis of glycogen and protein enzymes, that have great buffering capabilities and in long duration exercises based on aerobic energy exchange, there is synthesis of mitochondrial proteins" (PDF 525 / p.514).

**Why it works** — The mechanism is local metabolites acting as specific inducers (see [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]): "It is most certain that the specificity is determined by the local accumulation of metabolites, acting as inductors of synthesis of a limited number of proteins" (Viru, 289; PDF 526 / p.515). The result: "the muscles acquire the functional properties corresponding to (adequate for) the work regime," either faster anaerobic ATP resynthesis and contraction, more respiratory ATP resynthesis and endurance, or more contractile protein and strength, "or in the end result, to some degree of development of all of these qualities" (PDF 526 / p.515). Even new mitochondria take the load's character: "the ability of mitochondria to oxidize pyruvic acid in training for endurance is two times higher than in speed training (Yakovlev, 144)" (PDF 526 / p.515).

**When to apply** — Choose the session's dominant regime by the protein you want built. Inference: for a football lineman a heavy strength day (contractile protein) and a repeat-sprint day with short rest (buffering capacity) aim at different machinery, which supports keeping each session's main emphasis clear.

**When NOT to apply** — Table 1 is a four-row summary from Viru's 1995 book, with no data, loads or durations; it names a primary product, not the only one. The speed row says speed training builds sarcoplasmic reticulum, but the next page also has speed training increasing "muscle mass and thickness of the fibers," myofibril protein, "sarcoplasmatic proteins and myoglobin" (PDF 526 / p.515), so the rows overlap in practice. The "two times" pyruvate figure is a single citation without units or method. `supported`, not `proven`, under this book's rule for findings shown without data.

**Example** — The book's own pair (PDF 526 / p.515): under endurance exercise, fibre thickness "practically does not change" while mitochondrial number and area rise significantly; under speed exercise, fibre thickness always rises and sarcoplasmic reticulum proteins rise "substantially," while mitochondria rise "less than under the influence of exercises for endurance."

**Related** — [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--endurance-training-builds-mitochondrial-protein-without-hypertrophy]], [[claim--strength-hypertrophy-dilutes-mitochondria-and-speeds-endurance-fatigue]], [[framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy]] (1.13, the authors' hypertrophy types), [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]

The text below the table restates it by exercise type: "In strength exercises, the myofibril protein synthesis appears to be foremost. **What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.4, PDF 528 / p.517, checked against the page image): "In strength training (in contrast to endurance training) reworking of the contractile fibers takes place in the skeletal muscles without a corresponding increase in synthesis of the mitochondrial proteins and with adequate increases in the vascularisation of the muscle tissues. As a result, there is expressed hypertrophy, an increase in muscle mass of the tissues and a decrease in specific density in the mitochondria (Wenger et al, 292, MacDougall et al., 241, Tesch, Lindeberg, 273). This leads to a decreased supply of oxygen in the muscle tissues, a decrease in the functional power of the mitochondrial system and as a result, to increased production of lactate and as a consequence, fast fatigue in endurance loads (Tesch, Lindeberg, 273, MacDougall et al., 239, Meerson, Pshennikova, 78, Pshennikova, 99)."

**Why it works** — The chain on the page: contractile protein grows, mitochondrial protein does not keep pace, so the same mitochondria are spread through more muscle; less oxygen is used per unit of tissue, more lactate is made, and fatigue comes sooner in endurance work. Translation note: the page prints "with adequate increases in the vascularisation," but the "decreased supply of oxygen" that follows only makes sense if vascularisation does not keep up. Inference: probably "without adequate increases."

**When to apply** — When a strength phase precedes or overlaps a conditioning target in an athlete who needs repeated efforts: plan for the hypertrophy to cost some local oxidative capacity unless conditioning work is kept in. Eric's review: the baseline treats this kind of pairing as a programming constraint: "Compatible qualities are trained together; the rest are trained at a retention dose." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: this page gives one mechanism for why heavy hypertrophy work and endurance work compete.

**When NOT to apply** — The effect is dilution from hypertrophy; it does not apply to strength gains made with little size gain. Within this book the authors elsewhere cite research that strength training raises haemoglobin and myoglobin and helps distance sports ([[claim--strength-training-raises-haemoglobin-myoglobin-and-aids-distance-sport]], 4.4). The two are not the same claim: 4.4 is about strength training's net effect on distance performance, 9.1 is about mitochondrial density after "expressed hypertrophy." Record the difference; it is not marked `contested`. The cited studies (MacDougall, Tesch and Lindeberg, Wenger) are named but their data are not shown here.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own contrast, same page and the next: strength training gives "expressed hypertrophy" and lower mitochondrial density, whereas "training for endurance is not combined with general hypertrophy of the skeletal muscles and an increase in the myofibril mass" but with "an expressed increase in the number and size of the mitochondria" (PDF 528-529 / p.517-518).

# What Breaks Down During Work Decides What Is Built After It: Metabolites Induce Adaptive Protein Synthesis, Hormones Amplify It

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, citing Yakovlev and Viru throughout (9.1 §1.4, PDF 524 / p.513, checked against the page image): "Synthesis of proteins is provided for by the genetic program coordinated in the nucleus of the cell. Its realization activates the action of the inductors." "The basic inductors appear to be the cell metabolites (products of substance exchange in the cells) and hormones, reaching the cells via the blood." "Metabolites determine the specific character of the protein synthesis; synthesized are those proteins which are primarily destroyed, and likewise enzymes catalyzing biochemical reactions, lying in the base of the corresponding functions." "Hormones as a rule strengthen adaptive protein synthesis, inducted by metabolites." His summary: "the catabolic processes that take place in the muscles during the time of work determine the specific character of the following biosynthesis of the substances destroyed during muscular activity, that is, the specificity of the anabolic processes that take place in the post work period" (PDF 524 / p.513). He repeats it in 1.5: "Metabolites accumulated at the time of work, acts as inductors of adaptive protein synthesis. Hormones actively secreted in these conditions strengthen protein synthesis, specifically directed by metabolites, and assures the supplying of this process by 'constructive materials'" (PDF 528 / p.517).

**Why it works** — Two supporting pieces on PDF 527 / p.516. Gene repression: the muscle fibre carries the genes for all its proteins, but "part of the genetics can be 'repressed'"; under "trophic influence of the nervous system or some kind of change in the conditions, the existing suppression can be lifted and then the muscle can synthesize the proteins, which before this, were not capable of being synthesized" (Yakovlev, 144). Glucocorticoids: they mobilise protein, create "a reserve of free amino acids for ensuring the plastic functions," and move amino acids from one tissue to another, so "the plastic reserves of the cells can be exhausted in some tissues because of the stronger slow of plastic materials" (printed so; Inference: probably "outflow") "and in others as a consequence of more intense use of free resources in the anabolic processes" (Viru). Footnote 9 (PDF 528, quoting Viru 1995, ch. 8) gives the proposed signal: "low molecular weight products of protein degradation" acting on transcription, with specific activation if they "are protein specific fragments."

**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky draws the programming rule from it (PDF 532 / p.521): "Training can be considered effective when the loads bring about induction of adaptive protein synthesis in the desired direction. The criteria for such loads should (or can) be the accumulation of metabolites or the changes in the hormonal ensemble, necessary for specific induction of the adaptive synthesis of protein and for its strengthening (Viru, 289)." Inference: pick the session's means so the breakdown it causes is the breakdown of the structures you want rebuilt.

**When NOT to apply** — The section is a review of cited work (Viru, Yakovlev, Booth, Poortemans and others) with no data on the page. Inference: modern muscle biology also gives a large role to mechanical signalling, which this metabolite-and-hormone account does not mention, so treat it as one part of the mechanism. The page names no practical measure of "the accumulation of metabolites" or "the hormonal ensemble," so the effective-load criterion cannot be applied directly in a weight room.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own strength case (PDF 528 / p.517): hypertrophy from strength training "is based on the strengthened protein synthesis ... and is combined with an increase in the protein content, in mainly the myofibrils," and "the anabolic acting androgenic hormones strengthen this aggregate change (Viru, 33)."

**Related** — [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]], [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]], [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]]

# Strength Training Also Builds the Connective Tissue Around Muscle Fibres, and Too Much of It Can Make Muscles Thick and Less Fit for Fine, Varied Movement

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, citing Yakovlev (144) for each point (9.1 §1.4, PDF 528 / p.517, checked against the page image): "In a loaded muscle, there is an especially strong break-up of proteins in the isometric regime, and at the time of rest, their synthesis is more significantly displayed. But, besides the synthesis of the contractile muscle fibers there is intense protein synthesis of the connective tissue surrounding the muscle fibers. For muscle work, these excessively developed connective tissue layers not only are not needed, but are even harmful: the muscles become thick, unsuitable for different fine, varied and precise variations in their activity." The same paragraph gives a non-contractile change in the other direction: "Strength training leads mainly to a significant increase in the content of the elastic myostromins in the muscles, structural proteins taking part in muscle relaxation," which "serves to more fully and quickly relax the muscles after their contraction." Footnote 10 (PDF 528) glosses myostromin as "a protein found in muscle stroma, the supporting framework of muscle."

**Why it works** — The page gives the observation and its consequence, not a mechanism. Inference: the link to the isometric regime suggests long, high-tension holds are the case where the connective-tissue response is largest, since that is where Yakovlev reports the strongest protein breakdown and later synthesis.

**When to apply** — Inference: in sports where fine, fast and varied muscle control matters (throwing, striking, skill positions), weigh large volumes of heavy isometric or slow high-tension work against that need, and keep speed and skill work alongside it. This matches the authors' wider point that hypertrophy is not a goal in itself for most athletes.

**When NOT to apply** — One citation, no data, no dose: the page does not say how much training produces "excessively developed" connective tissue, nor how the "fine, varied and precise" loss was measured. The myostromin point cuts the other way (better relaxation after strength training), so the page does not support a blanket warning against strength work. Rated `untested`. Connective tissue around the fibres also transmits force and protects against strain injury (see [[principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle]]); this claim is about excess, not about connective tissue as such.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own picture of the end state: muscles that "become thick, unsuitable for different fine, varied and precise variations in their activity" (PDF 528 / p.517).

**Related** — [[claim--strength-hypertrophy-dilutes-mitochondria-and-speeds-endurance-fatigue]], [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]], [[framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy]], [[principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle]]

# Strength Training Also Builds the Connective Tissue Around Muscle Fibres, and Too Much of It Can Make Muscles Thick and Less Fit for Fine, Varied Movement

For muscle work, these excessively developed connective tissue layers not only are not needed, but are even harmful: the muscles become thick, unsuitable for different fine, varied and precise variations in their activity." The same paragraph gives a non-contractile change in the other direction: "Strength training leads mainly to a significant increase in the content of the elastic myostromins in the muscles, structural proteins taking part in muscle relaxation," which "serves to more fully and quickly relax the muscles after their contraction." # The Constructive Effect of Adaptation Has Three Bases and Works at Two Levels: Session Supercompensation and the Long-Term Delayed Training Effect

**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.5, "Essentials of the constructive effects of the adaptational process," Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519, checked against the page image): "The foundation for the development of the adaptational process in sports activity is the strengthened synthesis of structural and enzymatic proteins in the actively functioning cells." Strengthened protein synthesis "appears as a constructive effect of the adaptational process." "The basis for the constructive effect of adaptation lies in three phenomena (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 286):

# Restoration Procedures That Speed Metabolite Removal Remove the Signal for Protein Synthesis, So Rest Is Mainly for Synthesis, Not Readiness

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 531 / p.520, checked against the page image) ties the work-rest ratio to protein synthesis: "The after work activation of the nucleic acids and protein synthesis plays an important role in the formation of the structural 'footprints' in the specific response to the adaptation systems (Meerson, 76). This issue has a direct relationship to the extremely important practical problem - the ratio between work and rest." He then names "the prevailing presentation in practice and in the literature, of 'restoration' of the athlete after the training loads." "The problem is that the accelerated extraction from the body of the metabolites due to the use of different types of 'restorative' procedures, (that are widely recommended and used in sports practice) leads to a disturbance in protein synthesis and as a result, to a decrease in training effect of the loads and the specifics of its direction (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25)." "Thus, the rest period (or interval of time between the previous and following training session) is necessary not only for achieving a state of readiness (which to a significant extent, is evaluated subjectively) for the following portion of the training loads, but mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis (Verkhoshansky, 25, 26, 27)." His conclusion: "the metabolite dispersal from the body during the rest intervals, is in principle, not expedient because it liquidates the results of the previous load influence" (PDF 531 / p.520).

**Why it works** — The mechanism is his inducer model: metabolites formed during work are "the basic inductors of protein synthesis in the muscles" (PDF 531 / p.520; see [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]). Clear them early and the specific signal is gone. He adds that the after-effects, "structural 'footprints', traces," are what link one session to the next and "are maintained in the tissues, organs and systems of the athlete for several tens of hours" (PDF 531 / p.520).

**When to apply** — When deciding whether to use flushing-type recovery (massage, hydrotherapy, active recovery aimed at clearing metabolites) straight after a session whose adaptation you want. Eric's review: "Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)), and "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." (line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: Verkhoshansky's position supports managing recovery through load design rather than routine post-session modalities.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested`: the book contradicts itself on the same claim. In 6.9.3 the authors report that swimmers using restoration procedures systematically during voluminous loading gained 24.2% in absolute strength and 18.9% in strength-endurance, against 7.7% and 4.9% without them (Kuchnyev 1977; PDF 368 / p.357, as quoted in [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]]). In 8.6 Talyshev's sauna and hydrotherapy at 6-9 hours after the workout produced next-day supercompensation (PDF 462 / p.451, as quoted in [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]]). 9.1 calls metabolite dispersal "in principle, not expedient" with no qualifier for timing or dose. Inference: the two can be partly reconciled if procedures delayed until synthesis has run are allowed, but 9.1 does not say so. The page gives no data of its own, only his books (refs 24-27). Inference: "several tens of hours" is not a protocol; it gives no window per quality.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own statement of the priority: the rest interval is "mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis," and only secondarily for readiness, which "to a significant extent, is evaluated subjectively" (PDF 531 / p.520).

**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]] (6.9.3 and 8.6), [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]] (8.6), [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[framework--bauer-kasnacheev-energy-and-plastic-flows-fig-1]]

# Restoration Procedures That Speed Metabolite Removal Remove the Signal for Protein Synthesis, So Rest Is Mainly for Synthesis, Not Readiness

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 531 / p.520, checked against the page image) ties the work-rest ratio to protein synthesis: "The after work activation of the nucleic acids and protein synthesis plays an important role in the formation of the structural 'footprints' in the specific response to the adaptation systems (Meerson, 76). This issue has a direct relationship to the extremely important practical problem - the ratio between work and rest." He then names "the prevailing presentation in practice and in the literature, of 'restoration' of the athlete after the training loads." "The problem is that the accelerated extraction from the body of the metabolites due to the use of different types of 'restorative' procedures, (that are widely recommended and used in sports practice) leads to a disturbance in protein synthesis and as a result, to a decrease in training effect of the loads and the specifics of its direction (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25)." "Thus, the rest period (or interval of time between the previous and following training session) is necessary not only for achieving a state of readiness (which to a significant extent, is evaluated subjectively) for the following portion of the training loads, but mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis (Verkhoshansky, 25, 26, 27)." His conclusion: "the metabolite dispersal from the body during the rest intervals, is in principle, not expedient because it liquidates the results of the previous load influence" (PDF 531 / p.520).

**Why it works** — The mechanism is his inducer model: metabolites formed during work are "the basic inductors of protein synthesis in the muscles" (PDF 531 / p.520; see [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]). Clear them early and the specific signal is gone. He adds that the after-effects, "structural 'footprints', traces," are what link one session to the next and "are maintained in the tissues, organs and systems of the athlete for several tens of hours" (PDF 531 / p.520).

**When to apply** — When deciding whether to use flushing-type recovery (massage, hydrotherapy, active recovery aimed at clearing metabolites) straight after a session whose adaptation you want. Eric's review: "Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)), and "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." (line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: Verkhoshansky's position supports managing recovery through load design rather than routine post-session modalities.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested`: the book contradicts itself on the same claim. In 6.9.3 the authors report that swimmers using restoration procedures systematically during voluminous loading gained 24.2% in absolute strength and 18.9% in strength-endurance, against 7.7% and 4.9% without them (Kuchnyev 1977; PDF 368 / p.357, as quoted in [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]]). In 8.6 Talyshev's sauna and hydrotherapy at 6-9 hours after the workout produced next-day supercompensation (PDF 462 / p.451, as quoted in [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]]). 9.1 calls metabolite dispersal "in principle, not expedient" with no qualifier for timing or dose. Inference: the two can be partly reconciled if procedures delayed until synthesis has run are allowed, but 9.1 does not say so. The page gives no data of its own, only his books (refs 24-27). Inference: "several tens of hours" is not a protocol; it gives no window per quality.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own statement of the priority: the rest interval is "mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis," and only secondarily for readiness, which "to a significant extent, is evaluated subjectively" (PDF 531 / p.520).

# Start the Next Session When the Previous Session's Protein Synthesis Ends or Begins to Fall, Not Sooner and Not Much Later

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, citing Viru (289, 290, 291) (9.1 §1.5, PDF 532 / p.521, checked against the page image): "it is important to give attention to the need for determining the best time (moment) for the repeat work, in relation to the time of development of the post training protein synthesis. In other words, each following training session (or training load portion) must be started only at the moment when the protein synthesis, ensured by the preceding training session, is finished, or when the intensity of this protein syntheses start to decrease. If the following training session is carried out sooner (or too late), the main part of the positive influence of the preceding training session will not by realized" (printed so; the sense is "be realized"). He presents this, with the case against restoration procedures and complex loads, as grounds to "review the obsolete principles of training load organization in microcycle coming from the conception of Periodization of Training, introduced by L.Matveev, and working out contemporary models of programming the microcycle" (PDF 532 / p.521).

**Why it works** — The rest interval exists "mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis" (PDF 531 / p.520; see [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]). Load again while synthesis is still rising and the new breakdown cuts it short; wait until long after it has ended and the after-effects that link sessions, which last "several tens of hours" (PDF 531), have faded.

**When to apply** — When spacing sessions that load the same structures or quality, such as two heavy lower-body days or two speed-endurance sessions in a week. Inference: Fig 5 on PDF 533 (animal stress data, not training) shows protein synthesis peaking at about 24 and falling back toward baseline by 120-168 on its time axis (see [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]]); if that axis is hours, it would put the next hard session for the same tissues somewhere after the first day and well before a week. The page itself gives no hours.

**When NOT to apply** — No time windows, no measures and no data are given, and protein synthesis cannot be read in the field, so the rule needs a proxy that the page does not supply. It also says nothing about sessions aimed at different qualities, which load different proteins (see [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]]). Rated `untested`. Inference: in an in-season football week the game fixes most of the spacing, so the rule matters most in the off-season.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own failure case: a session "carried out sooner (or too late)" than the end or decline of the previous session's synthesis loses "the main part of the positive influence of the preceding training session" (PDF 532 / p.521).

**Related** — [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]] (8.6, timing by when work capacity is next needed), [[framework--periodization-as-additive-chain-vs-programming-as-hierarchical-whole]]
