# Periodization Treats Training as a Chain of Microcycles; Programming Treats It as a Hierarchical Whole Whose Key Unit Is the Great Adaptive Cycle

**What it is** — Footnote 14 (9.1 §1.5, PDF 532-533 / p.521-522, checked against the page images; the footnote runs from the foot of PDF 532 onto the foot of PDF 533 and is unsigned) explains the two conceptions the main text names when it calls for "contemporary models of programming the microcycle, based on the conception of Programming of training (Verkhoshansky, 27)" (PDF 532). "The difference between the two conceptions Periodization and Programming is based on the different 'vision' of the training process and different approach to its planning."
- Periodization: "the training process is seen as 'the chain of the microcycles', that is, an additive formation, 'the whole' which is 'the sum of its parts'. The microcycle represents its base structural element." The plan is "'constructed' from these microcycles, as from the 'bricks' of the different calibre, situated in an undulant tier on the axle of the time toward the date of the competition." On competition day "we were unable to predict the level of the athlete's performance, but we must assure its constant (persistence, incessant) increase and we must try to obtain the maximal 'angle' of this increase" (PDF 532).
- Programming: "the training process is seen as the hierarchical system of training influences on the organism, organised over time, which can only be diversified within the microcycles. So, the training process is the 'whole' which 'is greater than the sum of its parts'. Each change in the contents and in the sequence of microcycles changes 'the whole', provoking the phenomenon of 'emergence' (new properties arising in systems as a result of the interactions at an elemental level). So, the most important temporal measure of the training process is not the microcycle, but the Great Adaptive Cycle. A microcycle represents the working forms of the organization of the temporary parts of the general volume of the loads (necessary to reach the planned final result); the tier of which is determined by the general strategy of their distribution over time" (PDF 533).

**Why it works** — The argument rests on interaction: if what a microcycle does depends on what came before and after it (as the after-effects and delayed effects in 9.1 imply), then microcycles cannot be designed one at a time and stacked. Inference: this is the same non-additivity point the authors make with their "algebraic relations" for training order in Chapter 4 (see [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]).

**When to apply** — When building an annual or off-season plan: set the overall distribution of the load volume needed for the target result first, and let the microcycles follow from it, rather than picking standard microcycle templates per period and laying them end to end. Eric's review: Eric's stated model is "waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: that is a week-level pattern repeated over a block, closer to the microcycle-as-brick view this footnote criticises, though a four-week wave can also be read as a planned whole.

**When NOT to apply** — The footnote states a view; it gives no evidence that programming plans beat periodization plans. It does not define the "Great Adaptive Cycle" here (no length, no structure on these pages). Its author is not named, and it reads as a later editorial note explaining Verkhoshansky's position; treat it as his school's view. Its picture of periodization is the critic's version; the periodisation entries in this library carry the reply (see [[claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov]]). Rated `untested`.

**Example** — The footnote's own image of the old approach (PDF 532 / p.521): microcycles as "bricks" of different calibre laid "in an undulant tier on the axle of the time toward the date of the competition," with the aim of the steepest possible rise.

**Related** — [[principle--mesocycle-not-microcycle-as-the-unit-and-planned-dips-are-not-errors]] (6.8.1, the same rejection of the microcycle as the unit), [[claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov]] (6.3), [[framework--pasm-laws-of-adaptation-to-temporal-forms-of-training-fig-3]], [[claim--matveev-sports-form-phases-derive-from-prokop-adaptation-energy-phases]], [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]] (4.1.2), [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]]

"The difference between the two conceptions Periodization and Programming is based on the different 'vision' of the training process and different approach to its planning."
- Periodization: "the training process is seen as 'the chain of the microcycles', that is, an additive formation, 'the whole' which is 'the sum of its parts'. The microcycle represents its base structural element." The plan is "'constructed' from these microcycles, as from the 'bricks' of the different calibre, situated in an undulant tier on the axle of the time toward the date of the competition." On competition day "we were unable to predict the level of the athlete's performance, but we must assure its constant (persistence, incessant) increase and we must try to obtain the maximal 'angle' of this increase" (PDF 532).
- Programming: "the training process is seen as the hierarchical system of training influences on the organism, organised over time, which can only be diversified within the microcycles. So, the training process is the 'whole' which 'is greater than the sum of its parts'. Each change in the contents and in the sequence of microcycles changes 'the whole', provoking the phenomenon of 'emergence' (new properties arising in systems as a result of the interactions at an elemental level). So, the most important temporal measure of the training process is not the microcycle, but the Great Adaptive Cycle. # After a Single Stress, Protein Synthesis First Falls, Then Rises Well Above Baseline for Much Longer Than It Was Depressed (Meerson, Fig 5)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky opens the "consequent (second) phenomenon of the constructed effect of adaptation," supercompensation (9.1 §1.5, PDF 533 / p.522, checked against the page image). "If during the time of muscular work the processes of breakdown and oxidation dominate, that is, processes necessary for energy provision, then during the time of rest, restoration of that which was used up is required. The program of synthesis taking place during the time of rest is determined by the type of break-up reaction which took place during the time of work. In this way, any kind of break-up reaction brings about productive resynthesis reactions in the body (rule of V.Engelgard). In this way, in normal functioning biosystems the restorative process is always potentially greater and supersedes the processes of breakdown (the phenomena of supercompensation)." Then the evidence: "a onetime stress influence of the catabolic phase is followed by an anabolic phase, that is, generalized activation of nucleic acid and protein synthesis" (Meerson, 76, 77), and in "a one time emotional-painful stress type influence (trials on animals)" Figure 5 shows protein synthesis after the stress. "It has been established that the stage of post stress activation of the biosynthesis of RNA and protein, is first of all many times longer than the stage of biosynthesis depression and secondly, it is characteristic to see a substantial increase from the initial level" (PDF 533 / p.522).

Figure 5 ("Dynamics of the protein synthesis in myocardium (1), brain (2) and liver (3) after the stress (Meerson, 1986)," PDF 533, values read from the image): all three curves drop at once to a trough at the "8" mark (about 64 for myocardium, 61 for brain, 57 for liver), cross 100 before the "24" mark, and peak at 24 (about 163, 158 and 181). By 48 they are near 137, 141 and 127; by 120 near 115, 118 and 107; by 168 near 107, 110 and 100. The axes carry no labels. Inference: 100 is the pre-stress level, and 8, 24, 48, 120 and 168 are hours (168 hours is one week); the time axis has breaks after 24, 48 and 120.

**Why it works** — The page explains it by the genetic apparatus: the anabolic phase "can potentiate realization of the interrelationships between the functions and the genetic apparatus," so "the structural consequences are formed in the systems, specifically answering to the adaptation to a definite factor" (PDF 533 / p.522). The paragraph closes at the top of PDF 534 / p.523: this stage gives "a sufficiently long period of preparation during which the organs and systems can respond to the physiological loads faster," with changes "much greater than can be produced in conditions of sharp loads in the absence of an increased fund of prepared ribosomes" (Meerson, 76). The sentence introducing Fig 5 is garbled in translation ("right after the catabolic effect in all the studied organs, the laws of development in the activation of biosynthesis and an increase in content RNA which in turn, leads to the biosynthesis of protein"). Inference: it means that after the catabolic effect all the organs studied showed activated biosynthesis and higher RNA content, which then drove protein synthesis.

**When to apply** — As the shape to expect after a single hard stimulus: a short dip, then a long overshoot. Inference: it supports spacing repeat loads for the same tissues so they land on the overshoot, not the dip (see [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The data are from animals under "emotional-painful" stress, in heart, brain and liver, not skeletal muscle after training; the time course cannot be carried over to a training session without testing. Sample size and units are not given. `supported` for the pattern only. The rule that restoration "is always potentially greater" than breakdown is the supercompensation claim that the book contests elsewhere (see [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] and [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]]); Fig 5 shows overshoot of synthesis rate, not of stored content.

**Example** — Liver in Fig 5 (PDF 533 / p.522): synthesis falls to about 57% of baseline at 8, overshoots to about 181% at 24, and is back to about 100% by 168.

**Related** — [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (1.16), [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]

16:**What it is** — Verkhoshansky opens the "consequent (second) phenomenon of the constructed effect of adaptation," supercompensation (9.1 §1.5, PDF 533 / p.522, checked against the page image). "If during the time of muscular work the processes of breakdown and oxidation dominate, that is, processes necessary for energy provision, then during the time of rest, restoration of that which was used up is required. The program of synthesis taking place during the time of rest is determined by the type of break-up reaction which took place during the time of work. In this way, any kind of break-up reaction brings about productive resynthesis reactions in the body (rule of V.Engelgard). In this way, in normal functioning biosystems the restorative process is always potentially greater and supersedes the processes of breakdown (the phenomena of supercompensation)." Then the evidence: "a onetime stress influence of the catabolic phase is followed by an anabolic phase, that is, generalized activation of nucleic acid and protein synthesis" (Meerson, 76, 77), and in "a one time emotional-painful stress type influence (trials on animals)" Figure 5 shows protein synthesis after the stress. "It has been established that the stage of post stress activation of the biosynthesis of RNA and protein, is first of all many times longer than the stage of biosynthesis depression and secondly, it is characteristic to see a substantial increase from the initial level" (PDF 533 / p.522).
20:**Why it works** — The page explains it by the genetic apparatus: the anabolic phase "can potentiate realization of the interrelationships between the functions and the genetic apparatus," so "the structural consequences are formed in the systems, specifically answering to the adaptation to a definite factor" (PDF 533 / p.522). The paragraph closes at the top of PDF 534 / p.523: this stage gives "a sufficiently long period of preparation during which the organs and systems can respond to the physiological loads faster," with changes "much greater than can be produced in conditions of sharp loads in the absence of an increased fund of prepared ribosomes" (Meerson, 76). The sentence introducing Fig 5 is garbled in translation ("right after the catabolic effect in all the studied organs, the laws of development in the activation of biosynthesis and an increase in content RNA which in turn, leads to the biosynthesis of protein"). Inference: it means that after the catabolic effect all the organs studied showed activated biosynthesis and higher RNA content, which then drove protein synthesis.
22:**When to apply** — As the shape to expect after a single hard stimulus: a short dip, then a long overshoot. Inference: it supports spacing repeat loads for the same tissues so they land on the overshoot, not the dip (see [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]]).
24:**When NOT to apply** — The data are from animals under "emotional-painful" stress, in heart, brain and liver, not skeletal muscle after training; the time course cannot be carried over to a training session without testing. Sample size and units are not given. `supported` for the pattern only. The rule that restoration "is always potentially greater" than breakdown is the supercompensation claim that the book contests elsewhere (see [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] and [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]]); Fig 5 shows overshoot of synthesis rate, not of stored content.
26:**Example** — Liver in Fig 5 (PDF 533 / p.522): synthesis falls to about 57% of baseline at 8, overshoots to about 181% at 24, and is back to about 100% by 168.
28:**Related** — [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (1.16), [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]

# What Breaks Down During Work Decides What Is Built After It: Metabolites Induce Adaptive Protein Synthesis, Hormones Amplify It

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, citing Yakovlev and Viru throughout (9.1 §1.4, PDF 524 / p.513, checked against the page image): "Synthesis of proteins is provided for by the genetic program coordinated in the nucleus of the cell. Its realization activates the action of the inductors." "The basic inductors appear to be the cell metabolites (products of substance exchange in the cells) and hormones, reaching the cells via the blood." "Metabolites determine the specific character of the protein synthesis; synthesized are those proteins which are primarily destroyed, and likewise enzymes catalyzing biochemical reactions, lying in the base of the corresponding functions." "Hormones as a rule strengthen adaptive protein synthesis, inducted by metabolites." His summary: "the catabolic processes that take place in the muscles during the time of work determine the specific character of the following biosynthesis of the substances destroyed during muscular activity, that is, the specificity of the anabolic processes that take place in the post work period" (PDF 524 / p.513). He repeats it later in 1.4: "Metabolites accumulated at the time of work, acts as inductors of adaptive protein synthesis. Hormones actively secreted in these conditions strengthen protein synthesis, specifically directed by metabolites, and assures the supplying of this process by 'constructive materials'" (PDF 528 / p.517).

**Why it works** — Two supporting pieces on PDF 527 / p.516. Gene repression: the muscle fibre carries the genes for all its proteins, but "part of the genetics can be 'repressed'"; under "trophic influence of the nervous system or some kind of change in the conditions, the existing suppression can be lifted and then the muscle can synthesize the proteins, which before this, were not capable of being synthesized" (Yakovlev, 144). Glucocorticoids: they mobilise protein, create "a reserve of free amino acids for ensuring the plastic functions," and move amino acids from one tissue to another, so "the plastic reserves of the cells can be exhausted in some tissues because of the stronger slow of plastic materials" (printed so; Inference: probably "outflow") "and in others as a consequence of more intense use of free resources in the anabolic processes" (Viru). Footnote 9 (PDF 528, quoting Viru 1995, ch. 8) gives the proposed signal: "low molecular weight products of protein degradation" acting on transcription, with specific activation if they "are protein specific fragments."

**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky draws the programming rule from it (PDF 532 / p.521): "Training can be considered effective when the loads bring about induction of adaptive protein synthesis in the desired direction. The criteria for such loads should (or can) be the accumulation of metabolites or the changes in the hormonal ensemble, necessary for specific induction of the adaptive synthesis of protein and for its strengthening (Viru, 289)." Inference: pick the session's means so the breakdown it causes is the breakdown of the structures you want rebuilt.

**When NOT to apply** — The section is a review of cited work (Viru, Yakovlev, Booth, Poortemans and others) with no data on the page. Inference: modern muscle biology also gives a large role to mechanical signalling, which this metabolite-and-hormone account does not mention, so treat it as one part of the mechanism. The page names no practical measure of "the accumulation of metabolites" or "the hormonal ensemble," so the effective-load criterion cannot be applied directly in a weight room.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own strength case (PDF 528 / p.517): hypertrophy from strength training "is based on the strengthened protein synthesis ... and is combined with an increase in the protein content, in mainly the myofibrils," and "the anabolic acting androgenic hormones strengthen this aggregate change (Viru, 33)."

also('claim--compensatory-adaptation-is-temporary-and-precedes-stable-adaptation','Verkhoshansky\'s own paper restates the two layers in 9.1 §1.1, "Understanding compensatory adaptation" (PDF 521 / p.510, checked against the page image). The compensatory mechanisms are "dynamic and quickly rising physiological means of breakdown in order to provide for the body in extreme conditions and to gradually extinguish these means according to the amount of development of stable long term adaptation," so "they can be looked at as pre-adaptation appearances (Kusnetzov, 68)." Long-term adaptation "can have a progressive character if the training influence is stressful and brings about systematic disturbance of body homeostasis," and if the restructuring is "sufficiently substantial." also('principle--load-must-sit-within-the-current-adaptation-reserve-window','Verkhoshansky restates the rule in 9.1 §1.2 (PDF 522 / p.511, checked against the page image): "If the strength (magnitude), volume and duration of the training influences are below the necessary (optimal) amounts, CAR will not be realized; if they go above it, it leads to extreme exhaustion of the reserve capabilities. rel('framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation','[[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]] (9.1, Fig 4, the three-strategy version)')
also('framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation','Verkhoshansky\'s own paper redraws the two forms as strategies B and C of Fig 4 (9.1 §1.3, PDF 523 / p.512, values read from the image): over 20 weeks B rises to about 150% and C dips to about 80% near week 5, then finishes near 155%. It adds a third strategy, A, with low to moderate loads "for beginning and mid level athletes," in which "full exhaustion of CAR does not take place" (PDF 523). See [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]].')
rel('principle--mesocycle-not-microcycle-as-the-unit-and-planned-dips-are-not-errors','[[framework--periodization-as-additive-chain-vs-programming-as-hierarchical-whole]] (9.1, footnote 14), [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]] (9.1, the planned dip in strategy C)')
also('principle--mesocycle-not-microcycle-as-the-unit-and-planned-dips-are-not-errors','Footnote 14 of Verkhoshansky\'s paper (unsigned; PDF 532-533 / p.521-522, checked against the page images) makes the same move away from the microcycle: "the most important temporal measure of the training process is not the microcycle, but the Great Adaptive Cycle." rel('heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation','[[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]] (9.1, the protein-synthesis mechanism; rated contested against this entry\'s Kuchnyev data)')
also('heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation','Verkhoshansky\'s own paper gives the mechanism (9.1 §1.5, PDF 531 / p.520, checked against the page image): "the accelerated extraction from the body of the metabolites due to the use of different types of \'restorative\' procedures, (that are widely recommended and used in sports practice) leads to a disturbance in protein synthesis and as a result, to a decrease in training effect of the loads and the specifics of its direction." also('claim--complex-training-falls-short-for-highly-qualified-athletes','Verkhoshansky\'s own paper (9.1 §1.5, PDF 531-532 / p.520-521, checked against the page images) names the "principle of complexity" (footnote 11: "the training of all abilities - in the same training session or in the same microcycle"), considered progressive "30 years ago" (Osolin, Matveev, Platonov, Harre), and says "from the point of view of rationally directing the post training exchange processes in the body, it would not be possible to agree with a similar view today." Training should induce protein synthesis "in correspondence with the training task with the help of primarily single directed loads. \'Complex\' loads (especially, when these loads are used in the so-called \'developmental\' training sessions) are not advisable, because it is tied in with great, and (which is the essence of the matter), unjustified loss of energy, that does not ensure the specific effect of protein synthesis (Verkhoshansky, 26, 27)." Footnote 12: "\'Developmental\' training sessions are the training sessions with the high level loads." Unlike 6.12.2, these pages state no qualification limit: the objection is to the mechanism, not only to its use with highly qualified athletes. See [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]].')
rel('principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum','[[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] (9.1, LDTE as the long level of the constructive effect), [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]] (9.1, strategy C)')
also('principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum','Verkhoshansky\'s own paper places the LDTE as the second of "two levels of the constructive effect" (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519, checked against the page image): "The other level is related to the long stages of training. also('claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov','Verkhoshansky\'s own paper (9.1) adds two points to his side of the dispute. rel('claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation','[[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] (9.1), [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]] (9.1, Fig 5)')
also('claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation','Verkhoshansky\'s own paper uses supercompensation without the 1.16 reservation (both checked against the page images). # After a Single Stress, Protein Synthesis First Falls, Then Rises Well Above Baseline for Much Longer Than It Was Depressed (Meerson, Fig 5)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky opens the "consequent (second) phenomenon of the constructed effect of adaptation," supercompensation (9.1 §1.5, PDF 533 / p.522, checked against the page image). "If during the time of muscular work the processes of breakdown and oxidation dominate, that is, processes necessary for energy provision, then during the time of rest, restoration of that which was used up is required. The program of synthesis taking place during the time of rest is determined by the type of break-up reaction which took place during the time of work. In this way, any kind of break-up reaction brings about productive resynthesis reactions in the body (rule of V.Engelgard). In this way, in normal functioning biosystems the restorative process is always potentially greater and supersedes the processes of breakdown (the phenomena of supercompensation)." Then the evidence: "a onetime stress influence of the catabolic phase is followed by an anabolic phase, that is, generalized activation of nucleic acid and protein synthesis" (Meerson, 76, 77), and in "a one time emotional-painful stress type influence (trials on animals)" Figure 5 shows protein synthesis after the stress. "It has been established that the stage of post stress activation of the biosynthesis of RNA and protein, is first of all many times longer than the stage of biosynthesis depression and secondly, it is characteristic to see a substantial increase from the initial level" (PDF 533 / p.522).

Figure 5 ("Dynamics of the protein synthesis in myocardium (1), brain (2) and liver (3) after the stress (Meerson, 1986)," PDF 533, values read from the image): all three curves drop at once to a trough at the "8" mark (about 64 for myocardium, 61 for brain, 57 for liver), cross 100 before the "24" mark, and peak at 24 (about 163, 158 and 181). By 48 they are near 137, 141 and 127; by 120 near 115, 118 and 107; by 168 near 107, 110 and 100. The axes carry no labels. Inference: 100 is the pre-stress level, and 8, 24, 48, 120 and 168 are hours (168 hours is one week); the time axis has breaks after 24, 48 and 120.

**Why it works** — The page explains it by the genetic apparatus: the anabolic phase "can potentiate realization of the interrelationships between the functions and the genetic apparatus," so "the structural consequences are formed in the systems, specifically answering to the adaptation to a definite factor" (PDF 533 / p.522). The paragraph closes at the top of PDF 534 / p.523: this stage gives "a sufficiently long period of preparation during which the organs and systems can respond to the physiological loads faster," with changes "much greater than can be produced in conditions of sharp loads in the absence of an increased fund of prepared ribosomes" (Meerson, 76). The sentence introducing Fig 5 is garbled in translation ("right after the catabolic effect in all the studied organs, the laws of development in the activation of biosynthesis and an increase in content RNA which in turn, leads to the biosynthesis of protein"). Inference: it means that after the catabolic effect all the organs studied showed activated biosynthesis and higher RNA content, which then drove protein synthesis.

**When to apply** — As the shape to expect after a single hard stimulus: a short dip, then a long overshoot. Inference: it supports spacing repeat loads for the same tissues so they land on the overshoot, not the dip (see [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The data are from animals under "emotional-painful" stress, in heart, brain and liver, not skeletal muscle after training; the time course cannot be carried over to a training session without testing. Sample size and units are not given. `supported` for the pattern only. The rule that restoration "is always potentially greater" than breakdown is the supercompensation claim that the book contests elsewhere (see [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] and [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]]); Fig 5 shows overshoot of synthesis rate, not of stored content.

**Example** — Liver in Fig 5 (PDF 533 / p.522): synthesis falls to about 57% of baseline at 8, overshoots to about 181% at 24, and is back to about 100% by 168.

**Related** — [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (1.16), [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]

# Three Adaptation Strategies: Moderate Loads, High Loads Spread Evenly, High Loads Concentrated (Fig 4)

**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.3, "The adaptation strategy," Verkhoshansky defines strategy as "a form and means of realizing the laws of adaptation in practical sports conditions" and gives "three variants of adaptational strategy that have been studied and written up (figure 4)" (Verkhoshansky, 24; Verkhoshansky & Viru, 28, 286) (9.1 §1.3, PDF 522-524 / p.511-513, checked against the page images):
- **A, low-middle loads.** "If moderate volume and intensity training loads are used (in relation to the current state of the athlete) then for specialized workability (W) it is characteristic to have moderate and relatively balanced development." "Full exhaustion of CAR does not take place and the adaptational process is extended over time. This type of strategy is for beginning and mid level athletes." Afterwards W can go three ways: "a decrease (if there is a decrease in the strength of the training influences), stabilization (if so called maintenance loads are used) or further increases (if the strength of the training influences are increased)" (PDF 523 / p.512).
- **B, high loads distributed evenly**, "the traditional variant of organization of high level athlete training." It "ensures periodic short term disturbance of the constant internal body environment"; the process is "on a more intense level and its duration has a definite limit." Afterwards only two ways: "a decrease (even if the volume and intensity of the loads increases)" or "stabilization (if maintenance loads are used)" (PDF 523-524 / p.512-513).
- **C, high loads concentrated in a short period.** "The beginning stage of training is distinguished by systematic long term and deep disturbance of body homeostasis due mainly to the mobilization of the energy resources," seen as a "steady decrease in specialized workability (W)." Then, "as a result of mainly mobilization of the plastic resources," comes "a sharply expressed increase," to "a significant increase above the initial level and even the level achieved in the first two variants." Afterwards: "a decrease (if once again concentrated load volumes are used)" or "continued stabilization (if maintenance loads are used)" (PDF 524 / p.513).

Figure 4 (PDF 523 / p.512, values read from the image): panel A has no numeric scale. In B, W% rises from 100 to about 140 by week 10 and levels near 150 by week 20. In C, W% falls to about 80 near week 5, crosses 100 near week 9, and levels near 155 by about weeks 17-20. Each panel ends in tails a and b (A also c) after week 20. Hatched down-arrows mark the loading and open up-arrows the rebound.

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's mechanism is the energy-plastic alternation (see [[framework--bauer-kasnacheev-energy-and-plastic-flows-fig-1]]): in A "consecutive alternation of moderate activation of the energetic (solid line) and plastic (dotted line) reserves"; in B "the expenditure of the energetic resources (solid lines) is compensated for by the mobilization of the plastic resources (dash lines)"; in C a long energy-dominated phase is followed by a plastic-dominated phase (PDF 523-524). Figure note: the text refers to solid, dotted and dash lines, but the printed Fig 4 shows one curve per panel with hatched and open arrows and no line legend. Inference: the down-arrows stand for energetic mobilisation and the up-arrows for plastic mobilisation.

**When to apply** — Use A for beginners and mid-level athletes, where CAR need not be exhausted. Use C only where the athlete is highly qualified, the block can be protected from competition, and a planned dip in W is acceptable. In every variant, plan what follows the block: maintenance loads hold the level, and in B even more load does not raise it.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested` because the C-over-B claim is the same claim the existing 6.8.1 entry carries, which Issurin (2016) contests for team, combat and swimming sports (see [[framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation]]). Fig 4 is a schematic: there is no sample, sport or test named for W, and A has no scale. Inference: the planned dip of about 20% in C would collide with a competition schedule in a field sport. Eric's review: Eric's stated preference differs from both B and C: "waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: that is a difference in approach to record, not a conflict over the same claim.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own contrast in Fig 4 (PDF 523 / p.512): over the same 20 weeks, B rises steadily to about 150%, while C first drops to about 80% and then finishes near 155%.

**Related** — [[framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation]] (6.8.1, Fig 6.23, the two-form version with data), [[principle--mesocycle-not-microcycle-as-the-unit-and-planned-dips-are-not-errors]], [[claim--car-volume-is-capped-and-shrinks-as-mastery-nears-the-genetic-limit]], [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]]

# The Constructive Effect of Adaptation Has Three Bases and Works at Two Levels: Session Supercompensation and the Long-Term Delayed Training Effect

**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.5, "Essentials of the constructive effects of the adaptational process," Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519, checked against the page image): "The foundation for the development of the adaptational process in sports activity is the strengthened synthesis of structural and enzymatic proteins in the actively functioning cells." Strengthened protein synthesis "appears as a constructive effect of the adaptational process." "The basis for the constructive effect of adaptation lies in three phenomena (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 286):
- specificity of protein synthesis in the after work period, conditioned by the character of the work executed, its intensity and means of energy provision,
- supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins),
- a positive correlation between the catabolic and anabolic processes, brought about by the muscular work."

From these he names "two levels of the constructive effect." "One of them is related to the well known phase of restitution that is inherent in the phenomenon of supercompensation of products and energy used up in external work (Yakovlev, 139, 144, Viru, 289). The other level is related to the long stages of training. It is expressed in the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads, is known as the long term delayed training effect (Verkhoshansky, 23, 24, 25, 280, 281, 282, 283)" (PDF 530 / p.519).

**Why it works** — The short level rests on restitution: the phase after work "is characterized not only by increased metabolism but also a higher turnover speed of the muscle proteins which ensures the renewal of the molecular composition of the actin - myosin complex," clearing "'physiologically exhausted' structural 'footprints'" (Viru, 289, 291). "The program of biochemical changes ... determine the catabolic processes taking place in the muscles during the time of work. This program is realized during the time of rest" (PDF 530 / p.519). The long level is the same process summed over a concentrated block (see [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]).

**When to apply** — Inference: use the two levels to keep two time scales apart when judging a plan. A session or microcycle is judged by restitution over hours to days; a concentrated block is judged by the delayed rise weeks after the loading, not by how the athlete performs during it.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested` because the book contradicts itself on the second phenomenon. Here supercompensation covers "different structural and enzymatic proteins." In 1.16 the authors prefer "adaptive reconstruction," and printed p.88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" (as quoted in [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], PDF pp. 94-99). Same claim, same book. The page shows no data for either level. The link between the two levels (that the long-term effect is built from session-level restitution) is asserted, not shown.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own definition of the long level: "the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads" (PDF 530 / p.519), the pattern drawn as strategy C in Fig 4 (see [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]]).

**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]] (6.10), [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (1.16), [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the authors' names for effects on different time scales)

# The Constructive Effect of Adaptation Has Three Bases and Works at Two Levels: Session Supercompensation and the Long-Term Delayed Training Effect

**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.5, "Essentials of the constructive effects of the adaptational process," Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519, checked against the page image): "The foundation for the development of the adaptational process in sports activity is the strengthened synthesis of structural and enzymatic proteins in the actively functioning cells." Strengthened protein synthesis "appears as a constructive effect of the adaptational process." "The basis for the constructive effect of adaptation lies in three phenomena (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 286):
- specificity of protein synthesis in the after work period, conditioned by the character of the work executed, its intensity and means of energy provision,
- supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins),
- a positive correlation between the catabolic and anabolic processes, brought about by the muscular work."

From these he names "two levels of the constructive effect." "One of them is related to the well known phase of restitution that is inherent in the phenomenon of supercompensation of products and energy used up in external work (Yakovlev, 139, 144, Viru, 289). The other level is related to the long stages of training. It is expressed in the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads, is known as the long term delayed training effect (Verkhoshansky, 23, 24, 25, 280, 281, 282, 283)" (PDF 530 / p.519).

**Why it works** — The short level rests on restitution: the phase after work "is characterized not only by increased metabolism but also a higher turnover speed of the muscle proteins which ensures the renewal of the molecular composition of the actin - myosin complex," clearing "'physiologically exhausted' structural 'footprints'" (Viru, 289, 291). "The program of biochemical changes ... determine the catabolic processes taking place in the muscles during the time of work. This program is realized during the time of rest" (PDF 530 / p.519). Inference: the long level is the same process summed over a concentrated block; the page says only that it "is related to the long stages of training" (see [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]).

**When to apply** — Inference: use the two levels to keep two time scales apart when judging a plan. A session or microcycle is judged by restitution over hours to days; a concentrated block is judged by the delayed rise weeks after the loading, not by how the athlete performs during it.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested` because the book contradicts itself on the second phenomenon. Here supercompensation covers "different structural and enzymatic proteins." In 1.16 the authors prefer "adaptive reconstruction," and printed p.88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" (as quoted in [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], PDF pp. 94-99). Same claim, same book. The page shows no data for either level. The link between the two levels (that the long-term effect is built from session-level restitution) is asserted, not shown.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own definition of the long level: "the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads" (PDF 530 / p.519), the pattern drawn as strategy C in Fig 4 (see [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]]).

**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]] (6.10), [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (1.16), [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the authors' names for effects on different time scales)

# Restoration Procedures That Speed Metabolite Removal Remove the Signal for Protein Synthesis, So Rest Is Mainly for Synthesis, Not Readiness

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 531 / p.520, checked against the page image) ties the work-rest ratio to protein synthesis: "The after work activation of the nucleic acids and protein synthesis plays an important role in the formation of the structural 'footprints' in the specific response to the adaptation systems (Meerson, 76). This issue has a direct relationship to the extremely important practical problem - the ratio between work and rest." He then names "the prevailing presentation in practice and in the literature, of 'restoration' of the athlete after the training loads." "The problem is that the accelerated extraction from the body of the metabolites due to the use of different types of 'restorative' procedures, (that are widely recommended and used in sports practice) leads to a disturbance in protein synthesis and as a result, to a decrease in training effect of the loads and the specifics of its direction (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25)." "Thus, the rest period (or interval of time between the previous and following training session) is necessary not only for achieving a state of readiness (which to a significant extent, is evaluated subjectively) for the following portion of the training loads, but mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis (Verkhoshansky, 25, 26, 27)." His conclusion: "the metabolite dispersal from the body during the rest intervals, is in principle, not expedient because it liquidates the results of the previous load influence" (PDF 531 / p.520).

**Why it works** — The mechanism is his inducer model: metabolites formed during work are "the basic inductors of protein synthesis in the muscles" (PDF 531 / p.520; see [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]). Clear them early and the specific signal is gone. He adds that the after-effects, "structural 'footprints', traces," are what link one session to the next and "are maintained in the tissues, organs and systems of the athlete for several tens of hours" (PDF 531 / p.520).

**When to apply** — When deciding whether to use flushing-type recovery (massage, hydrotherapy, active recovery aimed at clearing metabolites) straight after a session whose adaptation you want. Eric's review: "Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)), and "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." (line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: Verkhoshansky's position supports managing recovery through load design rather than routine post-session modalities.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested`: the book contradicts itself on the same claim. In 6.9.3 the authors report that swimmers using restoration procedures systematically during voluminous loading gained 24.2% in absolute strength and 18.9% in strength-endurance, against 7.7% and 4.9% without them (Kuchnyev 1977; Platonov 1980; PDF 368 / p.357, as quoted in [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]]). In 8.6 Talyshev's sauna and hydrotherapy straight after the workout left next-day work capacity "below its initial level," which fits 9.1, but the same therapy 6-9 hours later produced next-day "significant increase (supercompensation)" (PDF 462 / p.451, as quoted in [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]]). 9.1 calls metabolite dispersal "in principle, not expedient" with no qualifier for timing or dose. Inference: the two can be partly reconciled if procedures delayed until synthesis has run are allowed, but 9.1 does not say so. The page gives no data of its own, only his books (refs 24-27). Inference: "several tens of hours" is not a protocol; it gives no window per quality.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own statement of the priority: the rest interval is "mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis," and only secondarily for readiness, which "to a significant extent, is evaluated subjectively" (PDF 531 / p.520).

**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]] (6.9.3 and 8.6), [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]] (8.6), [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[framework--bauer-kasnacheev-energy-and-plastic-flows-fig-1]]
